grades.quote: Code must lock the inode using ilock before reading or writing its metadata or content.
grades.reason: Describes the two mechanisms separately: iget/ref counts (a reference to an inode, released by iput) and ilock's sleep-lock for exclusive access to metadata and content. It also shows how the ref count keeps an inode alive in iput. It never says outright why the two are separate.

grades.quote: The file system uses struct inode reference counts as a kind of shared lock that can be held by multiple processes, in order to avoid deadlocks that would occur if the code used ordinary locks.
grades.reason: Directly explains the design. Inode reference counts act as a shared lock that many processes can hold, which avoids deadlocks that ordinary locks would cause. namex carries the directory inode forward with its ref count incremented but unlocked.

grades.quote: Another risk is deadlock. For example, next points to the same inode as ip when looking up ".". Locking next before releasing the lock on ip would result in a deadlock. To avoid this deadlock, namex unlocks the directory before obtaining a lock on next. Here again we see why the separation between iget and ilock is important.
grades.reason: Gives concrete reasons for separating iget (ref count) from ilock. The ref count keeps an inode from being deleted after the directory lock is released. Unlocking before locking next avoids self-deadlock on ".". It states the separation explicitly.
Covers general lock usage and granularity (big kernel lock, kalloc, per-file locks). It says nothing about inode reference counts or how they differ from inode locks.
